description: FIND-035 (iteration-12) correctly flagged that some worked-example tokens contained non-hex characters, contradicting REQ-010's `secrets.token_hex(5)` mechanism. The alphabet has now been fixed (every remaining concrete example token uses only [0-9a-f]), but a DIFFERENT, closely-related defect in the same examples was never caught and remains: `secrets.token_hex(5)` returns exactly 2*5=10 hex characters (verified: `python3 -c "import secrets; print(len(secrets.token_hex(5)))"` -> 10), but every single concrete worked-example token left in the current spec is only 9 hex characters long, one short. behavioral-spec.md:277 gives `"#c3d9a1e5f7"` -- the part after `#c` is `3d9a1e5f7`, which is 9 characters (verified by direct count: 3-d-9-a-1-e-5-f-7). verification-architecture.md:82/83 gives `"#c4f2a91b7c"` (`4f2a91b7c` = 9 chars) and `"#ca0b1c2d3e"` (`a0b1c2d3e` = 9 chars) -- both also 9, not 10. This is systematic across every remaining concrete example (3 for 3), not a one-off typo, meaning it was never actually cross-checked against the stated generation mechanism's real output length. An implementer or test-writer who treats these worked examples as the literal expected shape (e.g. writing a regex `^#c[0-9a-f]{9}$` for a sidecar/ledger validator, or a fixed-width string-slice assumption anywhere token length matters) will silently mismatch real `secrets.token_hex(5)` output, which is always exactly 10 hex characters after the `#c` prefix.

evidence.snippet: REQ-010 mechanism: `secrets.token_hex(5)` -> verified via python3 to always produce 10 hex chars. Worked examples: `#c3d9a1e5f7` (9 chars after #c), `#c4f2a91b7c` (9 chars), `#ca0b1c2d3e` (9 chars) -- all three concrete examples remaining in the spec are one character short of the stated mechanism's real output length
